Policy
Scope of Policy
This Clinical Policy Bulletin addresses magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) of the spine.
Note: Precertification may be required for select procedures and interventions. Use the CPT code search tool to see if precertification is required.
Medical Necessity
Aetna considers magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) of the spine medically necessary when any of the following criteria is met:
Clinical evidence of spinal stenosis; or
Clinical suspicion of a spinal cord or cauda equina compression syndrome; or
Congenital anomalies or deformities of the spine; or
Diagnosis and evaluation of lumbar epidural lipomatosis; or
Evaluation of recurrent symptoms after spinal surgery; or
Evaluation prior to epidural injection to rule out tumor or infection and to delineate the optimal anatomical location for performing the injection; or
Follow-up of evaluation for spinal malignancy or spinal infection; or
Known or suspected myelopathy (e.g., multiple sclerosis) for initial diagnosis when MRI of the brain is negative or symptoms mimic those of other spinal or brainstem lesions; or
Known or suspected primary spinal cord tumors (malignant or non-malignant); or
Persistent back or neck pain with radiculopathy as evidenced by pain plus objective findings of motor or reflex changes in the specific nerve root distribution, and no improvement after 6 weeks of conservative therapy Footnote1 * ; or
Primary spinal bone tumors or suspected vertebral, paraspinal, or intraspinal metastases; or
Progressively severe symptoms despite conservative management; or
Rapidly progressing neurological deficit, or major motor weakness; or
Severe back pain (e.g., requiring hospitalization); or
Spondylolisthesis and degenerative disease of the spine that has not responded to 4 weeks of conservative therapy Footnote1 * ; or
Suspected infectious process (e.g., osteomyelitis epidural abscess of the spine or soft tissue); or
Suspected spinal cord injury secondary to trauma; or
Suspected spinal fracture and/or dislocation secondary to trauma (if plain films are not conclusive); or
Suspected transverse myelitis.
Footnote1 * Conservative therapy = moderate activity, analgesics, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, muscle relaxants.
Experimental, Investigational, or Unproven
Aetna considers BoneMRI (MRI-based synthetic CT) experimental, investigational, or unproven for pre-operative assessments and surgical planning of the spine and the pelvis; and for diagnosing or monitoring of tumors (primary or metastatic).
Aetna considers MRI and CT of the spine experimental, investigational, or unproven for all other indications because their clinical value for indications other than the ones listed above has not been established. Clinical guidelines, including those from the Agency for Healthcare Policy and Research, have consistently recommended against routine imaging studies for acute low back pain.
Aetna considers the use of MRI for further evaluation of unstable injury in neurologically intact individuals with blunt trauma after a negative cervical spine CT result not medically necessary.
Aetna considers dynamic-kinetic MRI experimental, investigational, or unproven for evaluation of the cervical spine because its effectiveness has not been established.
Aetna considers the use of routine MRI after a normal CT of the cervical spine in obtunded or comatose individuals experimental, investigational, or unproven because the clinical value of this approach has not been established.
Aetna considers dual-energy CT experimental, investigational, or unrpoven for the evaluation of bone marrow edema and fracture lines in acute vertebral fractures because the clinical value of this approach has not been established.

Background
Due to its complexity, the spine is likely the most challenging part of the skeletal system to assess through radiological methods. Advances in computed tomography (CT) scanners and the introduction of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have significantly altered the approach to spinal diagnostic imaging. In the past, invasive techniques were necessary to gather information that can now be obtained through non-invasive technologies.
MRI of the spine utilizes a strong magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses—rather than ionizing radiation—to create high-contrast, multiplanar images that are particularly effective for evaluating intervertebral discs, the spinal cord, nerve roots, the epidural space, and ligaments. It is commonly employed when there is a suspicion of neurologic injury or ligamentous/soft-tissue pathology, such as in certain trauma cases where cord or ligament injuries are a concern. In contrast, CT of the spine is an X-ray-based, cross-sectional imaging technique that uses ionizing radiation to quickly produce high-resolution images of bony structures. In cases of acute blunt spinal trauma, multidetector CT is typically the first-line imaging modality due to its speed, availability, and accuracy in detecting and classifying fractures and assessing alignment, while MRI is reserved for specific inquiries, such as suspected neurologic or ligamentous injuries that are not fully characterized by CT (ACR, 2012; Expert Panel on Neurological Imaging, 2025).
Bulging intervertebral discs are present in more than half of all asymptomatic adults. Therefore, it is essential to conduct MRI or CT at the appropriate time and to interpret the results in light of clinical findings to ensure an accurate diagnosis and to prevent unnecessary treatment of conditions that may not be responsible for a patient's symptoms.
According to accepted guidelines, MRI is the preferred method of imaging for each of the medically necessary indications listed in the Policy section, with the exception of
suspected spinal fracture or dislocation due to trauma, where CT scan is the preferred method of imaging if plain films are inconclusive, and
evaluation of a patient with signs or symptoms of spinal stenosis, where MRI or CT are equally appropriate. For evaluation of recurrent symptoms after spinal surgery, MRI with and without gadolinium enhancement, is the preferred method of imaging.
Magnetic resonance imaging or CT evaluation of chronic mechanical low back pain (LBP) without radiculopathy or neurologic deficit, trauma, or clinical suspicion of systemic disorder (e.g., infectious process, metastatic disease) is not necessary unless back pain is severe (e.g., requiring hospitalization) or where symptoms are progressing despite conservative management (ICSI, 2002).
The American College of Physicians (2012) has recommended against obtaining imaging studies in patients with non-specific low back pain. In patients with back pain that cannot be attributed to a specific disease or spinal abnormality following a history and physical examination (e.g., non-specific low back pain), imaging with plain radiography, computed tomography (CT) scans, or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) does not improve patient outcomes. The American Academy of Family Physicians (2012) recommends against imaging for low back pain within the first six weeks unless red flags are present. Red flags include, but are not limited to, severe or progressive neurological deficits or when serious underlying conditions such as osteomyelitis are suspected. Imaging of the lower spine before six weeks does not improve outcomes but does increase costs. Low back pain is the fifth most common reason for all physician visits. The North American Spine Society (2013) has issued similar recommendations.
Cho et al. (2009) reported the results of a systematic review and meta-analysis of imaging strategies for low back pain (LBP) without indications of serious underlying conditions. Inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials that compared immediate, routine lumbar imaging (or routine provision of imaging findings) versus usual clinical care without immediate lumbar imaging (or not routinely providing results of imaging) for LBP without indications of serious underlying conditions. Primary outcomes were improvement in pain or function. Secondary outcomes included improvement in mental health, quality of life, patient satisfaction, and overall improvement. Outcomes were categorized as short-term (less than or equal to 3 months), long-term (greater than 6 months to less than or equal to 1 year), or extended (greater than 1 year). A total of six trials met the inclusion criteria: four assessed lumbar radiography, and two assessed MRI or CT. Duration of follow-up ranged from 3 weeks to 2 years. One trial excluded patients with sciatica or other symptoms of radiculopathy, and one did not report the proportion of patients with such symptoms. In the other four trials, the proportion of patients with sciatica or radiculopathy ranged from 24% to 44%. Three trials compared immediate lumbar radiography with usual clinical care without immediate lumbar radiography, and one compared immediate lumbar radiography with a brief education intervention plus lumbar radiography if no improvement was seen by 3 weeks. Patients (n = 1,804) enrolled in these trials had mainly acute or subacute (less than 12 weeks) LBP, and all trials were conducted in primary care or urgent care settings. Two studies assessed advanced imaging modalities. One study compared immediate MRI or CT with usual clinical care without advanced imaging in patients with mainly chronic LBP (82% had LBP for greater than 3 months) referred to a surgeon, whereas in the other study, all patients with LBP for less than 3 weeks underwent MRI, with randomization to routine notification of results within 48 hours versus notification of results only if clinically indicated. Patients were recruited from various settings (primary care, spine clinic, or emergency room). In both trials, the proportion of patients who underwent lumbar radiography before enrollment was not reported. The most frequent methodological shortcoming was the lack of (or unclear use of) blinded outcome assessment (5 of 6 trials), followed by inadequate description of the randomization method (4 of 6 trials). All trials excluded patients with features suggestive of a serious underlying condition, but exclusion criteria varied, and trials did not indicate the number of patients excluded because of such factors. The authors found no significant difference between routine, immediate lumbar imaging and usual clinical care without immediate imaging for improvement in pain or function at short-term or long-term follow-up. In the trial that reported extended (2-year) follow-up data, immediate MRI or CT was not better than usual clinical care without immediate imaging on either the EuroQol-5D (mean difference 0.02, 95% confidence interval: -0.02 to 0.07, 0 to 1 scale) or the SF-36 mental health score (-1.50, -4.09 to 1.09, 0 to 100 scale) in unadjusted analyses. The authors concluded that lumbar imaging for LBP without indications of serious underlying conditions does not improve clinical outcomes and that clinicians should refrain from routine, immediate lumbar imaging in patients with acute or subacute LBP and without features suggesting a serious underlying condition.
In a meta-analysis, Schoenfeld et al. (2010) examined whether adding an MRI would provide useful information that alters treatment when a CT scan reveals no evidence of injury in obtunded blunt trauma patients. Published studies from 2000 to 2008 involving patients undergoing MRI for further cervical spine evaluation after a "negative" CT scan were identified via a literature search of online databases. Data from eligible studies were pooled, and original scale meta-analyses were performed to calculate overall sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, likelihood ratios, and relative risk. The Q-statistic p-value was used to evaluate heterogeneity. A total of 11 studies met the inclusion criteria, yielding data on 1,550 patients with a negative CT scan after blunt trauma subsequently evaluated with an MRI. The MRI detected abnormalities in 182 patients (12%). Ninety traumatic injuries were identified, including ligamentous injuries (86/182) and fractures and dislocations (4/182). In 96 cases (6% of the cohort), the MRI identified an injury that altered management. Eighty-four patients (5%) required continued collar immobilization, and 12 (1%) required surgical stabilization. The Q-statistic p-value for heterogeneity was 0.99, indicating the absence of heterogeneity among the individual study populations. The authors concluded that reliance on CT imaging alone to "clear the cervical spine" after blunt trauma can lead to missed injuries. The findings of this study supported the addition of MRI in evaluating patients who are obtunded or unexaminable, despite a negative CT scan.
Callaghan et al. (2012) examined diagnostic practice patterns as an early step in identifying opportunities to improve the efficiency of care for patients with peripheral neuropathy. The 1996 to 2007 Health and Retirement Study Medicare claims-linked database was used to identify individuals with an incident diagnosis of peripheral neuropathy using International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, codes, requiring no previous neuropathy diagnosis during the preceding 30 months. Focusing on 15 relevant tests, these investigators examined the number and patterns of tests and specific test utilization 6 months before and after the incident neuropathy diagnosis. Medicare expenditures were assessed during the baseline, diagnostic, and follow-up periods. Of the 12,673 patients, 1,031 (8.1%) received a new International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, diagnosis of neuropathy and met the study inclusion criteria. Of the 15 tests considered, a median of 4 (interquartile range, 2 to 5) tests were performed, with more than 400 patterns of testing. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain or spine was ordered in 23.2% of patients, whereas a glucose tolerance test was rarely obtained (1.0%). Mean Medicare expenditures were significantly higher in the diagnostic period than in the baseline period ($14,362 versus $8,067, p < 0.001). The authors concluded that patients diagnosed with peripheral neuropathy typically undergo many tests, but testing patterns are highly variable. Almost 25% of patients receiving neuropathy diagnoses undergo high-cost, low-yield MRI, whereas few receive low-cost, high-yield glucose tolerance tests. Expenditures increase substantially in the diagnostic period. The authors stated that more research is needed to define effective and efficient strategies for the diagnostic evaluation of peripheral neuropathy.
Additionally, an UpToDate review on "Overview of polyneuropathy" (Rutkove, 2012) does not mention the use of MRI or CT in the diagnostic evaluation of individuals with polyneuropathy.
The Institute for Clinical Systems Improvement clinical practice guideline on "Adult acute and subacute low back pain" (ICSI, 2012) stated that imaging (CT, MRI, or X-ray) is not recommended for non-specific low back pain [strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence].
El Barzouhi et al. (2013) noted that MRI is frequently performed during follow-up in patients with known lumbar disk herniation and persistent symptoms of sciatica. The association between findings on MRI and clinical outcomes is controversial. These investigators studied 283 patients in a randomized trial comparing surgery and prolonged conservative care for sciatica and lumbar disk herniation. Patients underwent MRI at baseline and after 1 year. These researchers used a 4-point scale to assess disk herniation on MRI, ranging from 1 for "definitely present" to 4 for "definitely absent." A favorable clinical outcome was defined as complete or nearly complete disappearance of symptoms at 1 year. These investigators compared the proportions of patients with a favorable outcome among those with a definite absence of disk herniation and those with a definite, probable, or possible presence of disk herniation at 1 year. The area under the receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) curve was used to assess the prognostic accuracy of the 4-point scores regarding a favorable or unfavorable outcome, with 1 indicating "perfect discriminatory value" and 0.5 or less indicating "no discriminatory value." At 1 year, 84% of the patients reported having a favorable outcome. Disk herniation was visible in 35% of those with a favorable outcome and in 33% with an unfavorable outcome (p = 0.70). A favorable outcome was reported in 85% of patients with disk herniation and 83% without disk herniation (p = 0.70). Assessment of disk herniation by means of MRI did not distinguish between patients with a favorable outcome and those with an unfavorable outcome (area under ROC curve, 0.48). The authors concluded that MRI performed at 1-year follow-up in patients who had been treated for sciatica and lumbar disk herniation did not distinguish between those with a favorable outcome and those with an unfavorable outcome. Moreover, they stated that further research is needed to evaluate the value of MRI in clinical decision-making for patients with persistent or recurrent sciatica.
Steffens et al. (2014) systematically reviewed whether MRI findings of the lumbar spine predict future LBP in different samples with and without LBP. MEDLINE, CINAHL, and EMBASE databases were searched. Included were prospective cohort studies investigating the relationship between baseline MRI abnormalities of the lumbar spine and clinically important LBP outcomes at follow-up. These researchers excluded cohorts with specific diseases as the cause of their LBP. Associations between MRI findings and LBP pain outcomes were extracted from eligible studies. A total of 12 studies met the inclusion criteria; 6 studies presented data on participants with current LBP; 1 included a sample with no current LBP, 3 included a sample with no history of LBP, and 2 included mixed samples. Due to small sample size, poor overall quality, and the heterogeneity between studies in terms of participants, MRI findings, and clinical outcomes investigated, it was not possible to pool findings. No consistent associations between MRI findings and outcomes were identified. Single studies reported significant associations for Modic changes type 1 with pain, disc degeneration with disability in samples with current LBP, and disc herniation with pain in a mixed sample. The authors concluded that the limited number, heterogeneity, and overall quality of the studies do not permit definite conclusions on the association of MRI findings of the lumbar spine with future LBP.
Weber et al. (2015) evaluated the incremental diagnostic value of spine MRI evaluated separately from and combined with sacroiliac joint (SIJ) MRI in non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (nr-axSpA) compared with SIJ MRI alone. The study sample comprised two independent cohorts (A/B) of 130 consecutive patients aged less than or equal to 50 years with back pain, newly referred to two university clinics, and 20 healthy controls. Patients were classified according to clinical examination and pelvic radiographs as having nr-axSpA (n = 50), ankylosing spondylitis (n = 33), or non-specific back pain (n = 47). Four readers assessed SIJ and spine MRI separately 6 months apart, and 1 to 12 months later, both scans simultaneously using standardized modules. Readers recorded the presence/absence of spondyloarthritis (SpA) and their level of confidence in this conclusion on a 0 to 10 scale (0 = definitely not; 10 = definite). These researchers analyzed differences between SIJ MRI versus spine MRI alone, and SIJ MRI alone versus combined MRI, descriptively by the number/percentage of subjects according to the mean of four readers. In cohorts A/B, 15.8%/24.2% of patients with nr-axSpA having a negative SIJ MRI were reclassified as being positive for SpA by global evaluation of combined scans. However, 26.8%/11.4% of non-specific back pain controls and 17.5% of healthy volunteers with a negative SIJ MRI were falsely reclassified as having SpA by combined MRI. Low confidence in a diagnosis of SpA by SIJ MRI increased to high confidence by combined MRI in 6.6%/7.3% of patients with nr-axSpA. The authors concluded that combined spine and SIJ MRI added little incremental value compared with SIJ MRI alone for diagnosing patients with nr-axSpA and enhancing confidence in this diagnosis.
On behalf of the Tufts Medical Center Evidence-based Practice Center, Dahabreh and colleagues (2011) performed a systematic review of emerging MRI technologies for musculoskeletal imaging under loading stress for the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ). The review included 57 studies about MRI under physiologic loading stress performed in an upright or sitting position or under axial loading by using a compression device. The most commonly imaged regions were the spine (33 studies) and knee (13 studies). Most studies had a cross-sectional (n = 37) or case-control (n = 13) design and reported on anatomical measurements rather than patient-relevant endpoints. Studies were generally small: the median (25th, 75th percentile) number of case patients was 26 (17, 45), and the median (25th, 75th percentile) number of control participants was 13 (12, 20 for case-control studies). Fifteen of 57 studies used at least two imaging tests and reported on diagnostic or patient-relevant outcomes but did not provide meaningful information on the relative performance of the tests. In 10 studies that included information on adverse effects, 5% to 15% of participants reported new-onset or worsening pain and neuropathy during MRI under loading stress. The authors concluded that available evidence is insufficient to support the clinical utility of MRI under loading stress for musculoskeletal conditions.
Lord et al. (2014) reviewed the body of literature related to kinetic MRI (kMRI) of the cervical spine. A review of literature related to kMRI was performed using PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines. These researchers included 16 prospective and retrospective studies of symptomatic and asymptomatic patients who underwent kMRI of the cervical spine. The authors concluded that data suggested that kMRI is able to provide meaningful information regarding changes in the cervical spine in both normal and pathologic segments. Moreover, they stated that a prospective study comparing MRI and kMRI is needed to confirm the clinical utility of this technology.
Additionally, an UpToDate review on "Evaluation of the patient with neck pain and cervical spine disorders" (Isaac and Anderson, 2014) states that "Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should be the first-line imaging study performed in patients with progressive signs or symptoms of neurologic disease. MRI should also be obtained if there is a suspicion for infection or malignancy and if there are moderate to severe neck symptoms beyond six weeks, even if plain films are negative. A non-contrast MRI is sufficient in the majority of cases. The addition of gadolinium contrast intravenously allows better diagnosis of infection, tumor, or post-surgical epidural fibrosis and can be ordered subsequently if the non-contrast study is inconclusive." It does not mention the use of dynamic-kinetic MRI.
In a systematic review, Suri and colleagues (2015) examined whether lumbar muscle characteristics on MRI or CT can inform clinicians about the course of future LBP, functional limitations, or physical performance in adults with or without LBP. These investigators searched PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL through October 2014 for articles published in English in which authors assessed lumbar muscle characteristics on conventional MRI/CT as predictors of future LBP, functional limitations, or physical performance in adults. Studies with only post-surgical subjects were excluded. The search identified 3,554 articles, of which six observational cohort studies were included in the final review. These researchers used the Newcastle Ottawa Scale to evaluate potential bias. Data were extracted on study design, study population, sample size, participant characteristics, details of MRI/CT assessments, interventions, study outcomes, analysis methods, and study results. Because of heterogeneity between studies, these researchers conducted a qualitative evidence synthesis. Among high-quality studies, there was limited evidence that, for individuals with or without LBP, greater MRI-detected multifidus cross-sectional area at L5 to S1 predicted greater LBP intensity at 1-year follow-up, lesser erector spinae fat infiltration (FI) at L5 to S1 predicted greater LBP intensity at 15-year follow-up, and greater erector spinae side-to-side FI asymmetry at L3 to L4 predicted lower LBP frequency at 15-year follow-up; however, there was also limited evidence that all other MRI-detected paraspinal muscle characteristics examined were not predictive of LBP incidence, prevalence, frequency, or intensity at follow-up durations ranging from 1 to 15 years. There was limited evidence that greater CT-detected trunk muscle FI predicted worse physical performance in older adults at 3-year follow-up, but that trunk muscle cross-sectional area did not. The authors concluded that few lumbar muscle characteristics have limited evidence for an association with future LBP and physical performance outcomes, and the vast majority have limited evidence for having no association with such outcomes.
MRI / CT for Evaluation of Cervical Spinal Injury / Discontinuation of Cervical Collar Use
Veiga and Mitchell (2019) noted that a missed cervical spinal injury could have devastating consequences. Patients with a suspected cervical spinal injury are kept in rigid collars for cervical immobilization. Prolonged collar use has important clinical implications. A well-defined guideline related to the removal of cervical collars from adult obtunded blunt trauma patients has not been developed. These researchers determined if MRI offered a definitive benefit over CT with respect to patient management. They searched Ovid Online, EBSCO, NICE Evidence Journals, Medline, PubMed, BNI, CINAHL and Google Scholar as well as the grey literature. Data extraction and synthesis were performed on studies that compared the radiologic findings and clinical outcomes of CT scan and MRI in this patient group. There is evidence that supports the safe discontinuation of cervical collar use after a negative multi-detector CT scan result alone; MRI may detect a significant number of ligamentous injuries, but such injuries are rarely of clinical significance because they rarely alter clinical management. Its use should be limited to specific circumstances.
MRI for Evaluation of Whiplash and Non-Specific Neck Pain
Owens and colleagues (2018) stated that morphometric changes to cervical musculature in whiplash-associated disorder have been reported in several studies with varying results. However, the evidence remains unclear due to the limited number of cohorts studied, with one cohort reported in multiple publications. In a systematic review with meta-analysis, these researchers evaluated the evidence for cervical muscle morphometric changes on MRI following whiplash. They searched PubMed, Medline, and the Cochrane Library without language restrictions, using combinations of the MeSH terms "muscles," "whiplash injuries," and "magnetic resonance imaging." Studies of acute and chronic whiplash were included if they compared cervical spine muscle morphometry measurements from MR images between whiplash and control groups. The search identified 380 studies, and after screening, eight studies describing five cohorts (one acute, three chronic, and one both acute and chronic) met the inclusion criteria. Participant characteristics and outcome measures were extracted using a standard format, and the quality of eligible studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) and fat infiltrate (MFI) for acute and chronic whiplash cohorts were compared using mean difference (MD) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Meta-analysis models were created when data from more than two eligible cohorts were available, using inverse-variance random-effects models (RevMan5 version 5.3.5). The quality assessment was uniformly good, but only two studies blinded the assessor. Analysis of the acute cohorts revealed no consensus regarding CSA, and MFI was not measured in these cohorts. In chronic cohorts, CSA was probably increased in some muscles after whiplash, but there was insufficient evidence to confirm whether MFI was also increased. Due to limited data, meta-analyses were performed only for multifidus, revealing a significant increase in chronic whiplash multifidus CSA at C5 (Z = 3.51, p < 0.01) and C6 (Z = 2.66, p < 0.01), while MFI was significantly increased at C7 only (Z = 2.52, p < 0.01); however, the heterogeneity was unacceptably high (I² = 83%). The authors concluded that the strength of the evidence for cervical muscle morphometric changes on MRI after whiplash was inconsistent for both CSA and MFI, and they recommended that future study designs should standardize the quantification of three-dimensional muscle morphometry.
Farrell and colleagues (2019) noted that there is uncertainty regarding the clinical significance of findings on MRI in patients with whiplash-associated disorder (WAD) or non-specific neck pain (NSNP). In a systematic review and meta-analysis, these researchers compared the presence of cervical spine MRI findings in individuals with WAD or NSNP against pain-free controls. The subjects included adults with WAD (n = 994), NSNP (n = 715), or pain-free controls (n = 2,323). They searched Medline, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, SCOPUS, and Cochrane CENTRAL databases; two independent reviewers identified studies for inclusion and extracted data. The risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment Tool for Observational Cohort and Cross-Sectional Studies, and the overall quality of the evidence from the meta-analysis was assessed using the GRADE approach. Meta-analysis was performed using a random-effects model to calculate odds ratios (ORs) or standard mean differences (SMDs) for binary and continuous data. A total of 31 studies were included (eight comparing acute WAD to controls, 14 comparing chronic WAD to controls, and 12 comparing chronic NSNP to controls), comprising 4,032 subjects. The rectus capitis posterior major cross-sectional area (CSA) was found to be smaller in individuals with chronic NSNP than in controls (2 studies: SMD -1.18 [95% CI: -1.65 to -0.71]). The remaining meta-analysis comparisons showed no group differences in MRI findings. The quality of evidence was mostly low due to small sample sizes and high heterogeneity. The authors concluded that, given the typically low-quality evidence, definitive conclusions could not be drawn regarding the presence of MRI findings in individuals with WAD or NSNP compared to pain-free controls.
Furthermore, an UpToDate review on "Evaluation of the adult patient with neck pain" (Isaac and Kelly, 2019) states that "MRI imaging should be performed urgently in patients suspected of having an infection, malignancy, or spinal cord compression. In the absence of red flags, imaging is not necessary in patients with mild acute or chronic neck pain that does not limit or interrupt daily activities, does not affect performance of occupation, and is easily ignored when distracted. Patients who have undergone low-velocity neck trauma (e.g., whiplash) also generally do not require imaging." The review further states, "Imaging is indicated for patients with persistent moderate to severe neck pain (e.g., lasting >6 weeks and affecting sleep or ability to perform daily activities and/or occupation) even if they lack 'red flags.' For most of these individuals (e.g., without concern for infection or malignancy, no localizing neurologic symptoms or signs, no major trauma), the preferred initial examination is cervical spine radiography. If there are concerning abnormalities noted on cervical spine radiography (e.g., endplate erosion and soft tissue swelling raising concern about discitis/osteomyelitis, bony destruction raising concern about metastases, or bony remodeling suggesting an underlying mass), cervical spine MRI without contrast should be performed. MRI is generally not indicated if radiographs are normal or show only degenerative changes."
Computed Tomography-Guided Percutaneous Spine Biopsies for Determination of a Causative Organism in Cases of Suspected Infection
Sertic and colleagues (2019) noted that in cases of suspected spondylodiscitis and vertebral osteomyelitis, CT-guided biopsies are often performed to determine the causative organism and guide antimicrobial therapy. These researchers aimed to determine the diagnostic culture yield of CT-guided biopsies performed in cases of suspected spinal infections. A literature search of PubMed and Medline up to April 2017 was conducted using the keywords "CT guided vertebral biopsy infection," "CT-guided spine biopsy infection," "CT guided spine biopsy yield," and "CT guided vertebral biopsy yield." Inclusion criteria primarily consisted of studies exclusively using CT-guided biopsies in cases of suspected infectious lesions only. After study selection, published articles were analyzed to determine diagnostic culture yield, and descriptive statistics were applied. A total of 220 search results were screened, and 11 met the inclusion criteria and were reviewed. A total of 647 biopsies of suspected infectious spinal lesions were performed, with positive cultures obtained in 241 cases. Upon excluding one paper's skewed results, the net pooled culture yield was 33%. Several cultures grew multiple organisms, leading to a total of 244 species identified. The most commonly isolated organisms included Staphylococcus aureus (n = 83), coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (n = 45), and Mycobacteria (n = 38). The authors concluded that the diagnostic culture yield for CT-guided biopsies in cases of suspected spinal infection was low, approximately 33%. The reasons for this low yield were likely multifactorial and have not yet been clearly defined, including the effects of pre-administration of antibiotics, biopsy technique, inadequate sample volume, suboptimal specimen transfer methods, and culture techniques. These researchers stated that further study of these individual variables is needed, with a clearly defined and universally applied standard reference method. Considering that the administration of antibiotics is often delayed in an attempt to first determine a causative organism, the question of clinical utility is raised, especially given the potential consequences of doing so. Advances in technology and hospital policy regarding specimen acquisition, tissue transfer, and handling are needed to ensure that the benefits of CT-guided biopsies outweigh the risks. Collaboration between interventional radiologists and pathologists is essential to optimize these techniques and ensure optimal results.
The authors stated that the main drawback of this review was the heterogeneity of metrics in the 11 studies. Unfortunately, it was difficult to evaluate whether any particular variable, such as biopsy method or specimen transfer and processing method, had a statistically significant effect on diagnostic culture yield across multiple papers. Another major drawback was that nearly all included studies were retrospective reviews. Lastly, as there exists an imperfect gold standard for the diagnosis of vertebral osteomyelitis, there was considerable heterogeneity in how each study defined their reference method. Some studies employed a composite reference that included microbiological diagnosis or histopathology, radiological appearance, and clinical response to antimicrobial therapy, whereas others utilized positive microbiology or histopathology alone or heavily relied on clinician judgment. This not only made comparison between studies difficult but also complicated any measure of clinical sensitivity, specificity, or accuracy.
MRI / CT for the Diagnosis and Evaluation of Lumbar Epidural Lipomatosis
Ishikawa and associates (2006) stated that idiopathic symptomatic spinal epidural lipomatosis (SEL) is a rare condition, with few reports discussing diagnostic imaging criteria. These researchers examined factors related to clinical symptoms, correlations between clinical features and the presence of spinal epidural fat, and reviewed the literature concerning idiopathic SEL. Morphological gradings of epidural fat were assessed in seven patients with idiopathic SEL using MRI. Additionally, body mass index (BMI), the number of involved vertebral levels, grade, and pre-operative Japanese Orthopedic Association (JOA) scores were analyzed. Surgery resulted in symptomatic relief, with a mean JOA score recovery rate of 67.4%. Grading of epidural fat tended to show a slight negative correlation with pre-operative JOA scores, while a strong significant positive correlation was found between the number of involved vertebral levels and BMI. The authors concluded that the number of involved vertebral levels and obesity were strongly correlated, whereas the severity of dural compression was not always significantly associated with neurological complications. They indicated that epidural fat in the lumbar spine contributed to neurological deficits and suggested that weight-reduction therapy could decrease the number of vertebral levels involved. MRI-based grading was deemed helpful for the diagnosis and evaluation of idiopathic lumbar SEL, and symptoms and neurological findings were important for determining the surgical approach.
Gerardy and colleagues (2021) noted that SEL is characterized by excessive accumulation of normal fat in the epidural space. They presented findings from a retrospective study of 20 patients (17 men and 3 women) with an average age of 64 years, all suffering from radiculopathy and/or neurogenic claudication. Lipomatosis was idiopathic in six patients and secondary in 14 patients. MRI grading revealed grade-II lipomatosis in 30% of cases and grade-III in 70% of cases. All subjects improved following decompressive surgery via laminectomy and resection of epidural fat. The authors concluded that surgical decompression is a safe and effective procedure for patients with symptomatic lumbar epidural lipomatosis, particularly in cases of failed conservative treatment or neurological deficits.
Walker and co-workers (2021) stated that SEL is caused by an excess of adipose tissue accumulation localized to the thoracic and lumbar regions of the spine. While the exact pathogenesis remains unclear, the etiology of SEL can be broadly classified into five commonly associated risk factors: exogenous steroid use, obesity, endogenous steroid hormonal disease, spine surgery, and idiopathic disease. Progression of SEL may lead to neurological deficits, myelopathy, radiculopathy, neurogenic claudication, loss of sensation, difficulty voiding, lower extremity weakness, and, rarely, cauda equina syndrome. The diagnosis of SEL can be challenging, as symptoms often resemble other common conditions such as vertebral and disc disease. Diagnosis requires a high degree of clinical suspicion and various diagnostic modalities, with advanced imaging, specifically T1-weighted MRI, being the most sensitive test. Grading patterns of SEL were defined based on the epidural fat (EF) to spinal column (Spi C) index, with normal being less than or equal to 40%, and grading of SEL described as grade I, II, or III, with grade III characterized by an EF/Spi C index of greater than or equal to 75%.
Spinnato et al. (2022) noted that SEL is defined as the abnormal accumulation of unencapsulated adipose tissue in the spinal epidural space. SEL can be asymptomatic or cause a wide range of symptoms, the most common being neurogenic claudication. Other neurological manifestations may include myelopathy and radicular symptoms. The lumbar region is the most frequently involved spinal level, followed by the thoracic region. Imaging plays a crucial role in disease assessment, with MRI considered the most effective and sensitive modality for diagnosing and staging SEL; however, CT scans can also diagnose SEL. The diagnosis may be incidental in mild to moderate cases or considered in cases with neurological symptoms in moderate to severe disease. Recognized risk factors for SEL include exogenous steroid use and obesity, with recent studies finding associations between SEL and hyperlipidemia and liver fat deposition. SEL can be viewed as a spinal hallmark of metabolic syndrome. Initial treatment strategies focus on controlling risk factors (e.g., weight loss, cessation of steroid therapy), while surgical decompression may be necessary when conservative treatment fails or when acute/severe neurological symptoms develop.
Furthermore, an UpToDate review on “Polyradiculopathy: Spinal stenosis, infectious, carcinomatous, and inflammatory nerve root syndromes” (Rutkove and Tarulli, 2022) states that “Additional causes of spinal stenosis include congenital conditions, such as hereditary spinal stenosis or achondroplasia, systemic conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis or Paget disease, and excess accumulation of epidural fat (epidural lipomatosis), which can be seen in patients with Cushing disorder, exogenous glucocorticoid exposure, or obesity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has become the test of choice in the evaluation of spinal stenosis, although bony changes such as osteophyte formation are better demonstrated by computed tomography (CT).”
Upright MRI for Evaluation of the Spine
Kern et al. (2019) noted that the treatment of patients with spinal stenosis and concurrent degenerative spondylolisthesis is controversial, with two large randomized controlled trials (RCTs) reporting contradictory results. The researchers hypothesized that a substantial number of patients would show evidence of micro-instability after a sole decompression procedure. This study was a retrospective analysis of all cases of lumbar spinal stenosis treated at the Frankfurt University Clinic from 2010 through 2013. Patients with associated spondylolisthesis underwent upright magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies in flexion and extension to identify subtle signs of micro-instability. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the SF-36 bodily pain (BP) and physical functioning (PF) scales. A total of 21 patients were recruited for upright MRI studies, with a mean follow-up duration of 65 months (SD 16 months). Of these 21 patients, 10 (47%) showed signs of micro-instability, defined as movement greater than 4 mm on flexion/extension MRI. Comparison of mean SF-36 BP and PF scores between patients with and without micro-instability showed no statistically significant difference on either scale. The authors concluded that a substantial subset of patients developed morphological micro-instability after sole decompression procedures but did not experience any clinically significant effects from the instability.
Berry et al. (2019) stated that understanding changes in lumbar spine (LS) angles and intervertebral disc (IVD) behavior in end-range positions in healthy subjects could provide a basis for developing more specific LS models and comparing individuals with spine pathology. These researchers quantified three-dimensional (3D) LS angles and changes in IVD characteristics with end-range positions in three planes of motion using upright MRI in healthy individuals, determining which intervertebral segments contributed most in each plane of movement. A total of 13 participants (average age 24.4 years, range 18 to 51 years; 9 females; body mass index [BMI] = 22.4 ± 1.8 kg/m²) with no history of low back pain (LBP) were scanned in an upright MRI in various positions: standing, sitting flexion, sitting axial rotation (left, right), prone on elbows, prone extension, and standing lateral bending (left, right). Global and local intervertebral LS angles were measured, along with the anterior-posterior (AP) length of the IVD and the location of the nucleus pulposus. In the sagittal plane, lower LS segments contributed most to changes in position, with the nucleus pulposus migrating from a more posterior position in sitting flexion to a more anterior position in end-range extension. For lateral bending, the upper LS contributed most to end-range positions. Small degrees of intervertebral rotation (1 to 2°) were observed across all levels for axial plane positions, with no systematic changes in IVD characteristics for axial or coronal plane positions.
Papavero et al. (2020) stated that redundant nerve roots (RNRs) are a negative prognostic factor in patients with central lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS), with 40% of candidates for surgical decompression showing RNRs (RNR+) on pre-operative conventional MRI. In a retrospective observational study, these investigators examined the prevalence of RNRs in three functional postures (standing, neutral sitting, and flexed sitting) using upright MRI (upMRI). A total of 30 surgical candidates underwent upMRI, and sagittal and axial T2-weighted images of the three functional postures were evaluated. The segmental length of the lumbar spine (sLLS), lordotic angle (LA), and dural cross-sectional area (DCSA) were measured in each body position. Generalized linear mixed models were performed, with a significance level set at 0.05. The prevalence of RNRs decreased from 80% during standing to 16.7% during flexed sitting (p < 0.001). The sLLS increased significantly from standing to neutral sitting in both RNR groups (p < 0.001), while the increase from neutral sitting to flexed sitting was only significant (p < 0.001) for the group without RNRs (RNR-). The LA decreased significantly for both RNR groups from standing to flexed sitting (p < 0.001). The DCSA increased significantly in the RNR- group (p < 0.001) but not in the RNR+ group (p = 0.9). The authors concluded that the prevalence of RNRs was body position-dependent, and increases in DCSA played a determinant role in resolving RNRs.
Shaikh et al. (2020) examined the effect of upright, seated, and supine postures on lumbar muscle morphometry at multiple spinal levels and for multiple muscles. A total of six asymptomatic volunteers were imaged using a 0.5 T upright open MRI in seven postures (standing, standing holding 8 kg, standing 45° flexion, seated 45° flexion, seated upright, seated 45° extension, and supine), with scans at L3/L4, L4/L5, and L5/S1. Muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) and muscle position relative to the vertebral body centroid (radius and angle) were measured for the multifidus/erector spinae combined and psoas major muscles. Posture significantly affected the multifidus/erector spinae CSA, with a decrease in CSA from straight postures (standing and supine) to seated and flexed postures (up to 19%). Psoas major CSA significantly varied with vertebral level, showing opposite trends due to posture at L3/L4 (increasing CSA, up to 36%) and L5/S1 (decreasing CSA, up to 40%) with sitting/flexion. For both muscle groups, radius and angle followed similar trends, with a decreasing radius (up to 5%) and increasing angle (up to 12%) in seated/flexed postures. CSA and lumbar lordosis showed some correlation (multifidus/erector spinae L4/L5 and L5/S1, r = 0.37 to 0.45; psoas major L3/L4 left, r = -0.51). There was generally good repeatability (average ICC (3, 1): posture = 0.81, intra = 0.89, inter = 0.82). The authors concluded that changes in multifidus/erector spinae muscle CSA likely represented muscles stretching between upright and seated/flexed postures. For the psoas major, the differential level effect suggested that changing 3D muscle morphometry with flexion was not uniform along the muscle length. The muscle and spinal level-dependent effects of posture and spinal curvature correlation, including muscle CSA and position, highlighted the importance of considering measured muscle morphometry from different postures in spine models.
In an observational study, Rustagi et al. (2020) examined differences in spine structure measures between experimental postures and standard supine posture MRIs. A total of 34 patients with low back pain (LBP) were included, and MRIs were taken in six experimental postures. The dependent measures included sagittal view anterior (ADH), middle and posterior disc heights, thecal sac width, and left/right foraminal height (FH). In the axial view, measures included disc width and left and right foraminal height, assessed at L3/L4, L4/L5, and L5/S1. Each subject served as their own control, and spine measurements in the experimental posture were compared to the same measures in the standard supine posture. A 94% inter-observer reliability was observed. In the sagittal and axial views, 55 of the 108 and 11 of the 18 measures were significantly different. In the sagittal view:
ADH was significantly smaller in the sitting flexed posture by 2.50 mm ± 0.63 compared to the supine posture;
ADH in sitting neutral posture was significantly smaller than the standard posture by 1.97 mm ± 0.86;
sitting flexed posture showed that bilateral FH measures were significantly different;
Bilateral FH was larger in the sitting neutral posture compared to the standard supine posture by 0.87 mm ± 0.17.
The authors concluded that this research quantified the differences in spine structure measures that occurred in various experimental postures. The additional information gathered from an upright MRI may correlate with symptoms leading to an accurate diagnosis and assist in future spine research.
Bone Density Measurements on CT or MRI versus DEXA Scan
Ahmad et al. (2023) stated that novel methods of bone density assessment using CT and MRI have been increasingly reported in the spine surgery literature. Correlations between these newer measurements and traditional dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is unclear. In a systematic review, these investigators examined correlations between BMD from CT or MRI and DXA. Studies published between 2011 and 2021 that reported correlations between the CT- Hounsfield unit (HU) or MRI measurements to DXA t-scores or BMD of lumbar spine or hip were included in this systematic review. A total of 25 studies (15 CT, 10 MRI) met the inclusion criteria with a total number of 2,745 patients. The pooled correlation coefficient of spine CT-HU versus spine DXA, spine CT-HU versus hip DXA and spine CT-HU versus lowest t-score were 0.60, 0.50 and 0.60, respectively. Regarding spine DXA parameters, the pooled r2 for spine CT-HU versus spine t-score was 0.684 and spine CT-HU versus spine BMD was 0.598. In addition, in patients undergoing spine surgery in 4 studies, the pooled correlation between spine CT and spine DXA was (r2: 0.64). In MRI studies, the pooled r2 of spine MRI versus spine DXA and spine MRI versus hip DXA were -0.41 and -0.44, respectively. The authors concluded that CT-HU exhibited stronger correlations with DXA than MRI measurements. Lumbar CT-HU has the highest pooled correlation (r2 = 0.6) with both spine DXA and lowest skeletal t-score followed by lumbar CT-HU with hip DXA (r2 = 0.5), and lumbar MRI with hip (r2 = 0.44) and spine (r2 = 0.41) DXA. Both imaging modalities achieved only a moderate correlation with DXA. Few studies in both modalities have examined the correlation in spine surgery populations and the available data demonstrated that the correlations were worse in the degenerative spine population. A careful interruption of CT-HU and MRI measurement when evaluation of BMD as they only moderately correlated with DXA scores. At this time, it is unclear which modality is a better predictor of mechanical complications and clinical outcomes in spine surgery patients.
Osteoporotic Vertebrae Fracture Risk Measured by Quantitative Computed Tomography
In a systematic review and meta-analysis, Chen et al. (2023) compared the use of quantitative CT (QCT) and DXA in the evaluation of osteoporosis with vertebral fracture and osteoporosis without fracture. It has been reported that the volumetric BMD (vBMD) measured by QCT exhibits a stronger correlation with fracture risk than areal BMD (aBMD) measured by DXA. These investigators examined the ability of QCT and DXA to distinguish between osteoporosis with vertebral fracture and osteoporosis without fracture according to vBMD and aBMD. They carried out a primary literature search of the online databases up to July 3, 2022, in both English and Chinese publications, combining synonyms for "QCT", "DXA", and "osteoporosis". The Newcastle-Ottawa scale (NOS) was used to assess the quality of the selected articles. vBMD obtained via QCT and aBMD obtained via DXA were extracted, and were analyzed by Review Manager 5.4 and RStudio. A total of 6 studies with 610 individuals aged 45 to 90 years, of which 179 had vertebral fractures, were included in the final analysis. The weighted MD (WMD) between osteoporosis with vertebral fracture and osteoporosis without fracture for vBMD was - 27.08 (95% CI: - 31.24 to - 22.92), while for aBMD was - 0.05 (95% CI: - 0.08 to - 0.03). The authors concluded that both vBMD detected by QCT and aBMD detected by DXA could discriminate fracture status in the spine, and vBMD performed a stronger correlation with fracture risk.
Comparative Effectiveness of 4 Techniques for Identifying Vertebral Fragility Fractures
Ma et al. (2025) noted that the incidence of vertebral fragile fractures peaked among the elderly population, and identifying individuals at high risk of vertebral fractures and promptly instituting preventions are of critical importance. These investigators examined the effectiveness and values of Hounsfield unit (HU) values, vertebral bone quality (VBQ) scores, BMD measured by DXA, and QCT to discriminate between patients with and without vertebral fractures. They carried out a thorough search across PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, and Wan Fang Database to identify potential studies that met the eligibility criteria. Studies that examined the use of HU values, VBQ scores, QCT-measured BMD, and DXA-measured BMD in discriminating vertebral fractures were qualified. The combined results showed that there were significant differences in HU values, VBQ scores, QCT-measured BMD, and DXA-measured BMD between the fracture and non-fracture groups. Moreover, the pooled sensitivity, specificity, and AUC of HU values were 0.82, 0.67, and 0.76, respectively; the pooled sensitivity, specificity, and AUC of VBQ scores were 0.70, 0.75, and 0.78; the pooled sensitivity, specificity, and AUC of QCT-measured BMD were 0.85, 0.76 and 0.88. The authors concluded that all 4 methods, namely HU values, VBQ scores, QCT-measured BMD, and DXA-measured BMD can effectively distinguish between patients with and without vertebral fragile fractures. Among these, QCT-measured BMD exhibited a relatively high effectiveness in discriminating vertebral fractures. VBQ scores and HU values showed comparable effectiveness for discriminating vertebral fractures among elderly patients.
Imaging Techniques for Early Diagnosis and Management of Axial Spondyloarthritis
Jeon and Min (2024) presented recent finding of imaging studies employed for early diagnosis and management of patients with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA). Using low-dose whole spine CT (CT syndesmophyte score [CTSS]) improved diagnostic accuracy for evaluating spinal structural progression than previous method (modified Stoke Ankylosing Spondylitis Spinal Score [mSASSS]) in axSpA. The novel definition of positive finding of sacroiliac joint (SIJ) and spine MRI allowed diagnosis of axSpA earlier than plain radiography. Furthermore, novel MRI protocol such as volumetric interpolated breath-hold examination improved detection rate of structural change of axial joints in axSpA, Nuclear medicine imaging showed potential for diagnosis and predicting progression of axSpA. Ultrasonography (US)-guided injection is useful for controlling local joint pain of axSpA. AxSpA is characterized by pain and inflammation of axial joints such as the SIJ and spine. Detection of active inflammatory lesions using MRI has expanded the subtypes of axSpA to include non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA). Additionally, many other imaging techniques have improved, and can now detect structural and early inflammatory lesions of the axial joints. Furthermore, a method for quantitative measurement of syndesmophytes by CTSS has been developed; this method is more accurate and sensitive than the mSASSS for detecting spinal structural damage.
BoneMRI (MRI-Based Synthetic CT)
BoneMRI is an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled software that provides radiation-free, CT-like images through MRI scans for all spine and pelvic anatomies, with sub-millimeter quantitative equivalence to CT scans, for both adults and adolescents. It was cleared by the FDA via the 510(k) process. It can be used to visualize the bone structures in MRI images with enhanced contrast with respect to the surrounding soft tissues. It is used in the pelvis region, which includes the bony anatomy of the sacrum, hip bones, and femoral heads, as well as the lumbar spine region, which includes the bony anatomy of the vertebrae from L3 to S1. BoneMRI is not indicated for diagnosing or monitoring tumors (primary or metastatic).
Jans et al. (2021) examined the diagnostic performance of MRI-based synthetic CT (sCT) in detecting structural lesions in the sacro-iliac (SI) joints compared to routine T1-weighted MRI. These researchers found that sCT outperformed MRI in detecting erosions, sclerosis, and ankylosis, with higher sensitivity and specificity. The authors concluded that sCT could significantly enhance the diagnostic accuracy for patients suspected of having sacroiliitis, making it a valuable tool in clinical practice.
Morbee et al. (2021) examined the geometric measurements of MRI-based sCT of the lumbar spine in comparison to conventional CT for surgical planning. The study showed that sCT provided equivalent measurements for various bony structures, with excellent inter- and intra-reader reliability. The authors concluded that these findings supported the use of sCT as a viable option for surgical planning, offering the advantage of reduced radiation exposure while maintaining diagnostic accuracy.
Staartjes et al. (2021) examined the potential of MRI-based sCT for surgical planning in the lumbar spine, presenting a proof-of-concept (POC) study entailing 3 cases. The study showed that sCT could generate CT-like images from MRI data, allowing for accurate visualization of both normal and pathological structures. The results indicated that sCT could potentially reduce the need for traditional CT scans, thus minimizing radiation exposure. The authors concluded that sCT could be a valuable tool for surgical planning and intra-operative navigation in lumbar spine procedures.
Florkow et al. (2022) evaluated the accuracy of sCT in the 3D evaluation of hip joint morphology compared to conventional CT. This trial included 30 male patients; these researchers found that sCT measurements were statistically equivalent to those obtained from CT, with high inter-observer and intra-observer reliability. The authors concluded that these findings suggested that sCT could effectively examine hip morphology, providing a radiation-free alternative for clinical evaluations.
In a non-inferiority study, Van der Kolk et al. (2022) compared the image quality of deep learning (DL)-based sCT of the cervical spine to conventional CT. This trial involved 25 subjects and evaluated various bony structures. These researchers found that sCT was non-inferior to CT in terms of overall image quality and specific structural assessments. The authors concluded that these findings showed that sCT could visualize bony structures in the cervical spine, suggesting its potential as a radiation-free alternative to conventional CT.
Saveyn et al. (2022) discussed the potential of sCT images to enhance the evaluation of bony lesions on MRI, especially in the context of fracture assessment. The authors emphasized the need for further validation of synthetic CT in clinical practice, highlighting its promise in improving diagnostic accuracy for bony lesions while reducing radiation exposure associated with traditional CT imaging.
Morbee et al. (2022) examined the equivalency of MRI-based sCT to conventional CT in evaluating bony morphology of the hip joint. The study included adult patients who underwent both MRI and CT, with sCT images generated from MRI data. The results revealed strong agreement between sCT and CT measurements, indicating that sCT could serve as a reliable alternative for assessing hip morphology without the associated radiation exposure of CT. The authors concluded that these findings suggested that sCT may be beneficial for pre-operative assessments and surgical planning.
In a case-series study, Upadhyay et al. (2023) examined the use of sCT in evaluating lesions in children with rare musculoskeletal diseases. This study highlighted the ability of sCT to accurately identify musculoskeletal lesions in 2 patients, showing its potential as a non-radiative imaging modality. The authors concluded that these results suggested that sCT could be a valuable tool for monitoring musculoskeletal abnormalities in pediatric patients, especially in cases where traditional CT is limited due to radiation exposure concerns.
In a retrospective study, Morbee et al. (2023) determined the prevalence of incidental findings on SI joint MRI and the added value of MRI-based sCT in detecting these findings. This trial included 210 patients and found that incidental findings were more common than sacroiliitis, with sCT proving essential for diagnosing many lesions not visible on conventional MRI. The authors concluded that these findings underscored the importance of sCT in enhancing diagnostic accuracy and identifying clinically significant incidental findings. Moreover, these researchers stated that further quantitative research is needed to demonstrate the impact on the workflow, costs, and outcomes.
The authors stated that this study had several drawbacks. First, all subjects were imaged due to symptoms, giving these investigators no normal control group, although this resembled clinical practice. Second, only 210 subjects were included in this study, thus limiting the reporting of less frequent pathologies in the study population. Third, there was a risk of researcher bias, as the readers were aware of the objective of the study and reviewed MRI and sCT simultaneously for each case. In that way, the performance of sCT for detecting incidental findings could have been overestimated. Future studies should be designed to make diagnoses of incidental findings based on sCT and MRI separately. Fourth, in this study, no quantification or measurable data were available showing the impact of sCT on the workflow, costs, or outcomes. In addition, the MRI data were acquired with a high-performance 3-T MRI system, but it is not yet shown if similar image quality of sCT can be achieved with MRI systems of different field strengths and different technical performance; further studies are needed to compare the diagnostic performance of sCT with conventional CT.
In a cadaveric study, Davidar et al. (2023) presented a case showing the use of robot-assisted screw fixation using MRI-based sCT for radiation-free spine surgery. The study compared morphometric analyses of conventional CT and sCT scans, showing that sCT yielded comparable results in screw placement accuracy. The authors concluded that this study highlighted the potential of sCT to facilitate safe and effective surgical planning while minimizing radiation exposure.
Vereecke et al. (2023) examined the prevalence of anatomical variations of SI joints using MRI and sCT images in 215 patients suspected of sacroiliitis. The findings showed that 82.8% of the evaluated joints exhibited at least 1 anatomical variant, with the most common being the ilio-sacral complex and bipartite iliac bony plate. The study also identified a new variant, an accessory facet of the SI joint. Notably, the occurrence of these variants was associated with factors such as age, sex, and BMI. The authors concluded that these findings suggested that synthetic CT was effective in detecting subtle anatomical variations, which may represent subtypes of normal anatomy.
Shcherbakova et al. (2024) carried out a feasibility study on a short MRI protocol specifically designed for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS), which combines MRI and MRI-based sCT images to visualize both soft and bony structures in a single, radiation-free examination. This trial included 18 adult volunteers and examined the protocol’s ability to visualize critical anatomical landmarks needed for detecting 3D pathoanatomical changes and surgical planning. The authors concluded that the results indicated high precision and reliability in measurements, suggesting that this innovative protocol could enhance the study of scoliosis and improve surgical navigation.
Iwasaka-Neder et al. (2024) compared MRI-based sCT to conventional CT (cCT) for evaluating hip morphology and maturity in pediatric patients. This trial included 38 hips from 19 patients and showed that sCT provided equivalent measurements to cCT, with high inter- and intra-observer reliability. The accuracy of sCT in determining physeal maturity status was found to be 98.4%. The authors concluded that these findings suggested that sCT is a reliable alternative to cCT for evaluating hip morphology in children, offering the advantage of reduced radiation exposure.
Schiettecatte et al. (2024) examined the equivalency of MRI-based sCT to cCT in assessing the bony morphology of SI joints in children. The study included 10 participants and found that sCT provided good overall image quality and excellent agreement for various bony assessments. The authors concluded that by all the measures in a group of normal children, sCT was visually equivalent to CT for assessment of the bony morphology of pediatric SI joints. These researchers stated that in a clinical setting, adding sCT to the MRI protocol may have additional value as it allows for easily visually interpretable visualization of the bony structures of the SI joints in children without the use of ionizing radiation. Moreover, these investigators stated that future studies in larger groups of children, also including pathological scans of the SI joint, are needed to further examine the added value of sCT for assessment of structural lesions (erosions, ankylosis, and sclerosis) of sacroiliitis on sCT in pediatric SI joints in comparison with the classically used MRI sequences and CT as the gold standard where available.
The authors stated that this study had several drawbacks. The principal drawback was that these researchers did not image children with sacroiliitis; therefore, this trial was limited to assessing image quality for normal appearances and normal variation. Second, CT and MRI imaging did not take place on the same day; the additional MRI scan was obtained within approximately 1 month after the CT scan. Third, different kinds of CT, including PET-CT, were employed, depending on the clinical question.
Willesen et al. (2024) examined the effectiveness of MRI-based sCT in detecting new bone formation in patients with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) compared to low-dose CT (ldCT) and radiography. The study involved 17 patients and revealed that sCT showed high specificity and sensitivity for detecting structural changes, outperforming radiography. The authors concluded that these findings suggested that sCT could be a valuable tool for monitoring structural spine damage in axSpA patients, especially in clinical trials.
Krabbe et al. (2024) compared the detection of structural lesions in the SI joints using T1-weighted 3D spoiled gradient echo MRI and MRI-based sCT against conventional T1-weighted turbo spin echo MRI. This trial included 19 patients and found that both T1-weighted GRE and sCT improved sensitivity and reader confidence for detecting erosions, sclerosis, and ankylosis compared to T1-weighted TSE. The authors concluded that both 1-mm semi-coronal T1w-gradient echo (GRE) and 1-mm semi-coronal sCT increased sensitivity and reader confidence for the detection of erosion, sclerosis, and ankylosis, compared with standard 4 mm T1w-turbo spin-echo (TSE). These researchers stated that these methods might be a useful addition to SI joint MRI protocols both in routine clinical care and as structural outcome measures in clinical trials.
The authors stated that this study had several drawbacks. First, the sample size was small (n = 19), which limited the ability to reveal significant differences between methods; however, these investigators were able to show several statistically significant findings that suggested that improved image resolution with T1w-GRE and sCT are promising methods to improve the detection of structural lesions compared with lower resolution T1w-TS. Second, little training was provided to the readers to allow them to become acquainted with the different types of images and apply the scoring methodology, and all readers had little experience with the T1w-GRE and especially sCT images, which may have limited the inter-reader agreement. But strikingly, the inter-reader agreement was significantly higher or tended to be higher for T1w-GRE and sCT (images that were new to all readers) compared with T1w-TSE for most lesion types. Third, the study was not designed to have a reference standard; CT could have been used as such. However, even low-dose CT may be considered inferior to an optimized T1-weighted MRI protocol with sufficient resolution and tissue contrast, and CT was not carried out since it was not considered necessary for the objectives of this trial. In a few joints, ankylosis was detected by sCT with poor or moderate confidence, but not by T1w-GRE. These researchers were unable to prove if this represented true ankylosis or if it was a false-positive finding on sCT, which would correspond to a higher specificity of T1w-GRE. Fourth, these investigators employed the same lesion definitions as Jans et al. (2021) to reproduce the image assessment methodology of that study, well aware that other groups, including the ASAS MRI group, have slightly different wording of the definitions, e.g., the ASAS MRI group also discriminated between erosion and “fat metaplasia in an erosion cavity” (‘backfill’). This might have resulted in minor inconsistencies among the expert readers that were mostly used to applying the ASAS definitions; however, these investigators considered it unlikely to have had a major impact on the comparisons between sequences. Fifth, the study did not attempt to examine the accuracy or confidence in determining the absence of lesions, only their presence. Since no control subjects were included, readers may have had a bias toward detecting lesions with high sensitivity. The authors’ MRI protocol for T1w-TSE had a voxel size of 4.0 mm × 0.8 mm × 0.7 mm, whereas other institutions employ a lower slice thickness of 3 mm. In-plane resolution may also differ depending on local protocol optimization. It was possible that a higher resolution T1w-TSE might have increased sensitivity and reader confidence for detecting structural lesions, at the expense of extended scan time; therefore, these results may not be generalizable to centers that use a significantly higher resolution of T1w-TSE. Furthermore, these findings may not be generalizable to newly diagnosed bio-naive patients, who are likely to have somewhat less damage than the patients included in this trial, although these researchers expected the overall trends in lesion detection across imaging methods to be rather similar.
Michael et al. (2025) presented a case report detailing the use of MRI-generated sCT in the treatment of a 14-year-old male athlete with chronic bilateral spondylolysis. After unsuccessful non-operative management, the patient underwent a novel MRI that showed nonunion of the spondylolysis and persistent edema. Subsequently, he received minimally invasive bilateral L4 robot-navigated intra-laminar screw fixation, resulting in complete healing as confirmed by CT 3 months post-surgery. The authors concluded that this case highlighted the potential of MRI-generated sCT in pediatric spondylolysis management, providing a comprehensive assessment of bony and soft tissue pathology without the ionizing radiation associated with traditional CT.
Evaluation of Patients With Thoracolumbar Spine Trauma
The Congress of Neurological Surgeons’ systematic review and evidence-based guidelines on "The evaluation and treatment of patients with thoracolumbar spine trauma: Radiological evaluation" (Qureshi et al, 2019) stated that "there was insufficient evidence that MRI can help predict clinical outcomes in patients with acute traumatic thoracic and thoracolumbar spine injuries".
MRI and Cervical Spine Clearance of Neurologically Intact Patients With Blunt Trauma
In a meta-analysis, Malhotra and co-workers (2017) quantified the rate of unstable injuries detected by MRI that were missed on CT in blunt cervical spine (CS) trauma patients and evaluated the utility of MRI in CS clearance. These researchers conducted a systematic review of worldwide evidence across five major medical databases. Studies were included if they reported the number of unstable injuries or provided sufficient details for inference. Variables assessed included severity, CT/MRI specifications, imaging timing, and outcome/follow-up. Pooled incidences of unstable injury on follow-up, weighted by the inverse of variance among all included patients, both obtunded and alert, were reported. Of 428 unique citations, 23 were deemed eligible, involving 5,286 patients and reporting 16 unstable injuries across five studies. The overall pooled incidence was 0.0029%. Among studies reporting only obtunded patients, the pooled incidence was 0.017%, while in alert patients, it was 0.011%. All reported positive findings were critically reviewed, and only 11 could be considered truly unstable. The authors concluded that there was significant heterogeneity in the literature regarding the use of imaging after a negative CT. The finding rate for unstable injury on MRI was extremely low in both obtunded and alert patients. They stated that although MRI is frequently performed, its utility and cost-effectiveness require further study. Key points of this meta-analysis included the following: there were 16 unstable injuries on follow-up MRI among 5,286 patients, the positive finding rate among obtunded patients was 0.12%, and the positive finding rate among alert patients was 0.72%. MRI exhibited a high false-positive rate, and its utility necessitated further studies. The use and role of "confirmatory" tests showed wide variations.
Wu and associates (2018) noted that the use of MRI for cervical clearance after a negative cervical CT scan result in alert patients with blunt trauma who are neurologically intact is not infrequent, despite poor evidence regarding its utility. These investigators evaluated the utility and cost-effectiveness of using MRI versus no follow-up in this patient population. A modeling-based decision analysis was performed during the lifetime of a 40-year-old individual from a societal perspective. The two strategies compared were no follow-up and MRI. A Markov model with a 3% discount rate was used, incorporating parameters from the literature. Base cases, along with probabilistic and sensitivity analyses, were performed to assess the cost-effectiveness of the strategies. The cost of MRI follow-up was $11,477, with a health benefit of 24.03 quality-adjusted life-years (QALY); the cost of no follow-up was $6,432, with a health benefit of 24.08 QALY. No follow-up emerged as the dominant strategy, offering a lower cost and higher utility. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis indicated that no follow-up was the better strategy in all 10,000 iterations. This strategy remained superior regardless of the NPV of the initial CT result and continued to be the better option when the incidence of missed unstable injury resulting in permanent neurologic deficits was less than 64.2% and the incidence of patients immobilized with a hard collar who still sustained cord injury was greater than 19.7%. Multiple three-way sensitivity analyses were performed. The authors concluded that MRI is not cost-effective for further evaluation of unstable injury in neurologically intact patients with blunt trauma after a negative cervical spine CT result.
Dynamic Supine Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Xu and colleagues (2017) analyzed the current evidence regarding the role of dynamic supine MRI (dsMRI) in the evaluation of cervical spondylotic myelopathy. A total of 13 studies were identified through a comprehensive literature search performed in the PubMed, Embase, and ISI databases as fulfilling the inclusion criteria and were reviewed for subject characteristics, radiographic parameters, and salient findings. Studies reviewed suggested that dsMRI was able to detect new appearance or increased grade of medullary compression in greater than or equal to 20% of patients and to demonstrate an average narrowing of the cervical canal by 20% (in comparison with the neutral position). Several additional parameters were investigated, but their clinical significance remained unconfirmed; 2 studies examined how surgical decision-making could be affected by the additional findings of dsMRI. The authors concluded that dsMRI represents an available modification of conventional static MRI and is potentially able to demonstrate pathologies that might be previously missed. They stated that evidence suggested that dsMRI can elucidate spinal cord compression with higher sensitivity, resulting in improved diagnostic accuracy of cervical spondylotic myelopathy, which may impact surgical planning for these patients; however, more high-quality studies are needed to further establish its indications to avoid over-diagnosis with this powerful imaging technique.
Routine MRI after a Normal CT of the Cervical Spine in Obtunded or Comatose Individuals
Khanna and associates (2012) stated that the value of MRI in the evaluation of the obtunded or comatose patient with a potential neck injury is a controversial subject. Some authors have suggested that MRI of the cervical spine adds no value in the evaluation of patients with a normal CT of the neck. However, others have suggested that MRI is the gold standard for clearing the cervical spine in a clinically suspicious or unevaluable blunt trauma patient. These researchers examined their data in regard to these conflicting hypotheses. Five consecutive years of data from 17,000 patients seen at the authors’ Level I trauma center yielded 512 individuals who underwent both CT and MRI of the cervical spine. Of the latter group,150 individuals met 3 strict inclusion criteria for this study:
obtundation (Glasgow Coma Scale less than or equal to 13, with 94 of this group comatose [Glasgow Coma Scale less than or equal to 8]);
no obvious neurologic deficits; and
a normal cervical CT.
